# Week 7, Day 4.1 - Prerequisites check

**No new TypeScript today.** Today's difficulty is *ordering*, not syntax.

| In play | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `let` vs `const`, block scope | [week3/day2_1](/learn/w3/d2/p1) |
| Template literals | [week6/day3_1](/learn/w6/d3/p1) |
| `beforeAll` / `beforeEach` | [week3/day2_2](/learn/w3/d2/p2) |
| Objects as return values | [week3/day1_1](/learn/w3/d1/p1) |

One pattern is worth its own cell, because getting it wrong produces a confusing failure.

## Declare outside, assign inside

A value produced in a hook has to be visible to every test. So it is **declared** in the
`describe` scope with `let` and **assigned** inside the hook.

| Written | Result |
|---|---|
| `const id = ...` inside the hook | invisible to the tests - block-scoped |
| `let id = ""` outside, assigned inside | every test can read it |

`const` is impossible here: the value does not exist yet when the line runs.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Building a URL with a value in it

Two ways. Both work; one reads better once there is more than one piece.

| Style | Written |
|---|---|
| Concatenation | `BASE + "/Account/v1/User/" + userId` |
| **Template literal** | `` `${BASE}/Account/v1/User/${userId}` `` |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

parts.title: One response feeds the next request

blocks.text:
# Week 7, Day 4.2 - One response feeds the next request

To update something you need its id. To delete it you need its id. **The server invents the id**,
so you cannot write it down in advance - you have to create the thing, catch the id, and carry it
forward.

> **Mode: test-runner.** This part is about running specs with the Playwright test runner. The studio editor runs library code, so follow these along in your own checkout.

## The problem, stated once

| You want to test | You need |
|---|---|
| Update | an id that exists |
| Delete | an id that exists |
| Read one item | an id that exists |

Reusing an id you found by hand is the trap: someone else deletes that record and your suite
turns red for a reason that has nothing to do with your code. **Create your own, every run.**

## `beforeAll`, not `beforeEach`

| Hook | Runs | Here |
|---|---|---|
| `beforeEach` | before every test | six users created, five abandoned |
| **`beforeAll`** | once per describe | one user, used by all six |

The prerequisite is not part of what any test is checking, so it belongs in a hook - and it only
needs doing once.

## What each step showed

| Step | Point |
|---|---|
| 1 | the hook actually produced an id and a token |
| 2 | the id alone is **401** - not permission |
| 3 | the same request with `Authorization: Bearer` is 200 |
| 4 | the captured id used in a **body**, giving 201 |
| 5 | `PUT`, then **read it back** to prove the change |
| 6 | `DELETE` answers **204** with an empty body |

## Step 3, in detail: headers

The third thing a request can carry, and the one the session had to defer.

| Header | Says |
|---|---|
| `Content-Type: application/json` | the body I am sending is JSON - Playwright sets this from `data` |
| `Authorization: Bearer <token>` | here is my proof; I am allowed |
| `Accept` | the format I would like back |

```ts
await request.get(url, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });
```

Miss it and you get **401** - not a wrong answer, an unanswered question.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 5, in detail: assert the consequence

`PUT` returned 200. That only means the server accepted the instruction.

```ts
expect(response.status()).toBe(200);          // it accepted

const after = await request.get(...);          // now go and look
expect(isbns).toContain("9781491904244");      // the new one is there
expect(isbns).not.toContain(GIT_BOOK);         // the old one is gone
```

Both halves matter. Checking only that the new value appeared would pass even if the update had
*added* rather than *replaced*.

## Step 6, in detail: 204 has no body

`204 No Content` means done, nothing to say. So there is nothing to parse.

| Call | Result |
|---|---|
| `response.status()` | `204` |
| `await response.text()` | `""` |
| `await response.json()` | **throws** - an empty string is not JSON |

The session hits this live and has to delete the line. It is not a bug in the API and not a bug
in Playwright; it is what "no content" means.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## PUT or PATCH?

| Verb | Means | If you omit a field |
|---|---|---|
| `PUT` | replace the whole thing | it is **cleared** |
| `PATCH` | change what I send | it is left alone |

The session says developers treat them as interchangeable, and in practice many do. But the
difference is real and measurable - [week8/day1_2](/learn/w8/d1/p2) sends both to the same
record and shows a `PUT` wiping a field that `PATCH` preserved. Read the docs, then probe.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom |
|---|---|
| A hard-coded id from yesterday | red suite, unrelated cause |
| `beforeEach` for a one-time prerequisite | slow, and litter left on the server |
| `const` for a value assigned in a hook | it will not compile |
| `.json()` on a 204 | throws, and looks like an API fault |
| Trusting a 200 without reading it back | an update that did nothing still passes |

**Next:** [Day 4.3 - Where the setup should live](/learn/w7/d4/p3)

# Week 7, Day 4.3 - Where the setup should live

Same `beforeAll`, same header - arranged so it is written once for the whole suite.

## Four homes for setup, worst to best

| Where | Runs | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| Inside each test | every test | the same eight lines, forever |
| `beforeEach` | every test | a user per test, most abandoned |
| **`beforeAll`** | once per describe | good - but repeated in every *file* |
| **A fixture** | once, wherever asked | the real answer |

[day4_2](/learn/w7/d4/p2) is the third row. [day5_2](/learn/w7/d5/p2) takes the fourth step in two
stages: a plain function first, then a fixture.

240 lines versus 8, and 30 abandoned users versus 5. The abandoned-users column is the one that
gets you a stern email from whoever runs the sandbox.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Cleaning up is part of the design

| Where | Cleans up |
|---|---|
| `afterAll` | what the describe created |
| A fixture's teardown (after `use()`) | what the fixture created - automatically |

A fixture is better here too: teardown sits next to setup, so it is hard to forget one and not
the other.

```ts
account: async ({ request }, use) => {
  const created = await createAccount(request);
  await use(created);                       // the test runs here
  await deleteAccount(request, created);    // always, even if it failed
}
```

## Reviewer's checklist for an API suite

| Look for | Why |
|---|---|
| A hard-coded id or token | it will rot, and not on your schedule |
| A fixed username on a shared API | passes once, then collides forever |
| `.json()` near a `DELETE` | 204 has no body |
| A status assertion with no body assertion | [day2_2](/learn/w7/d2/p2) Step 6 |
| Something created and never deleted | you are a guest |
| A base URL spelled out in each test | one host change, many edits |

**Next:** [Day 4.4 - Practice](/learn/w7/d4/p4)

# Week 7, Day 4.4 - Practice

Delete whatever you create.

problems.statement:
**The full journey, your version**
Create a user, add two books, replace one, delete one, then delete the user - asserting the
consequence at every step.

**Right when:** every step asserts a status **and** reads something back, and the sandbox is left
as you found it.

**beforeEach, deliberately**
Change your `beforeAll` to `beforeEach` and count the users created.

**Right when:** you can say how many, how many were cleaned up, and why `afterAll` no longer
matches.

**Drop the header**
Remove `Authorization` from one authorised call.

**Right when:** you get 401 and can explain why that is different from 403 - look both up.

**Parse a 204**
Call `.json()` on a delete response.

**Right when:** you can quote the error and say what you should have asserted instead.

**PUT versus PATCH, measured**
Find an endpoint on this API that takes both, send each with a field missing, and compare.

> Hint: if you cannot find one, say so - that is a valid finding about this API.

**Right when:** you have either a measured difference or a documented reason there is none.

**A stale id**
Create a user, capture the id, delete the user, then use the id again.

**Right when:** you can name the status and say what it tells you about how the server checks the
token and the id.

**Prove the update replaced rather than added**
Write the weakest version of Step 5 - assert only that the new ISBN is present - then make the
update add instead of replace.

**Right when:** the weak test still passes while the behaviour is wrong, and your stronger version
catches it.
